quest01-calculator#1.en: Clear the calculator completely, so nothing is left in its memory.

quest01-calculator#2.en: Do it on the calculator below — press the keys yourself.

quest01-calculator#3.en: Clear-all lives under SHIFT 9 (CLR): SHIFT, 9, then 3 (All), then = to confirm.

quest01-calculator#5.en: Press SHIFT, then 9 — that opens the CLR menu.

quest01-calculator#8.en: Switch the frequency column (FREQ) ON, so you can record how often each value occurs.

quest01-calculator#9.en: Work through the SETUP menu on the calculator below.

quest01-calculator#10.en: Frequency lives in SETUP: SHIFT, MODE (SETUP), scroll ▼, 4 (STAT), then 1 (ON).

quest01-calculator#12.en: Press SHIFT, MODE to open SETUP.

quest01-calculator#13.en: Press ▼ to reach the second page.

quest01-calculator#15.en: Put the calculator into single-variable Statistics mode, ready to type a data set in.

quest01-calculator#16.en: Use the MODE menu on the calculator below.

quest01-calculator#17.en: MODE opens the list of modes: MODE, 3 (STAT), 1 (1-VAR).

quest01-calculator#21.en: Choose 1 (1-VAR) — now you can type the data.

quest01-calculator#22.en: Capture this data set on the calculator: ${list(data)}

quest01-calculator#23.en: Get into 1-VAR mode, then type each value. It’s done once all of them are in.

quest01-calculator#24.en: MODE, 3, 1 for 1-VAR. Type a value, then = (or ▼) to drop to the next row. Repeat for every number.

quest01-calculator#27.en: Type the first value, press = to move down a row.

quest01-calculator#28.en: Repeat until every value is entered.

quest01-calculator#29.en: The data ${list(data)} is already captured. Read off n — how many values there are.

quest01-calculator#30.en: Use the STAT → Var menu on the calculator below.

quest01-calculator#33.en: Press SHIFT, 1 to open the STAT menu.

quest01-calculator#36.en: The data ${list(data)} is already captured. Read off the mean (x̄).

quest01-calculator#42.en: The data ${list(data)} is already captured. Read off the standard deviation — use σx, not sx.

quest01-calculator#43.en: SHIFT, 1 (STAT), 4 (Var), 3 (σx), then =. (σx is option 3; sx is the wrong one.)

quest01-calculator#46.en: Choose 3 (σx) — the population standard deviation, not 4 (sx).

quest01-calculator#48.en: The data ${list(data)} is already captured. Use MinMax to read off the median.

quest01-calculator#49.en: Use the STAT → MinMax menu on the calculator below.

quest02-centre-spread#8.en: Which of these is a measure of ${ask === "spread" ? "spread (dispersion)" : "central tendency (centre)"}?

quest02-centre-spread#9.en: Spread tells you how scattered the data is.

quest02-centre-spread#10.en: Centre tells you a typical or middle value.

quest02-centre-spread#12.en:
Calculate the mean of:
${list(data)}${dp ? "
(round to 1 decimal place)" : ""}

quest02-centre-spread#13.en: Add all the values, then divide by how many there are.

quest02-centre-spread#15.en: The mean of ${n} values is ${m}. Calculate the sum of the values (Σx).

quest02-centre-spread#16.en: Rearrange x̄ = Σx / n into Σx = x̄ × n.

quest02-centre-spread#20.en: The data is already in order — the median is the middle value.

quest02-centre-spread#25.en: The mode is the value that appears most often.

quest03-quartiles#11.en: A data set has ${n} values arranged in order. What is the position of ${QLABEL[which]}?

quest03-quartiles#13.en: Use the position formula — it’s a fraction of (n + 1), not of n.

quest03-quartiles#17.en: Find the position first, apply the rounding rule, then count to that spot in the list.

quest03-quartiles#19.en: For a data set, Q1 = ${q1} and Q3 = ${q3}. Calculate the interquartile range (IQR).

quest03-quartiles#20.en: The IQR is the spread of the middle half — subtract the lower quartile from the upper.

quest03-quartiles#23.en:
An ordered data set:
${list(data)}
Calculate the IQR.

quest03-quartiles#25.en: Find Q1 and Q3 from the list first, then IQR = Q3 − Q1.

quest03-quartiles#28.en: For a data set, Q1 = ${q1} and Q3 = ${q3}. Calculate the semi-quartile range.

quest03-quartiles#29.en: The semi-quartile range is HALF the interquartile range: (Q3 − Q1) ÷ 2.

quest03-quartiles#41.en: the left edge of the box

quest03-quartiles#42.en: the right edge of the box

quest03-quartiles#45.en: read the value off the number line

quest03-quartiles#46.en: Read the ${name} off the box-and-whisker plot.

quest03-quartiles#47.en: Look at ${where}, then read straight down to the number line.

quest03-quartiles#48.en: The ${name} is ${where} — read it off as ≈ ${map[which]}.

quest03-quartiles#49.en: Tap the part of the plot that shows the interquartile range.

quest03-quartiles#50.en: the box — from Q1 to Q3

quest03-quartiles#52.en: Tap the section holding the lowest 25% of the data.

quest03-quartiles#54.en: Tap the section holding the highest 25% of the data.

quest03-quartiles#56.en: Tap the matching part of the box-and-whisker plot.

quest03-quartiles#57.en: The box is Q1→Q3 (the IQR); the line inside is the median; each whisker is a 25% tail.

quest03-quartiles#58.en: That is ${target.a}. Each of the four sections holds about 25% of the data.

quest03-quartiles#61.en: A data set has Q1 = ${q1} and Q3 = ${q3}. Calculate the ${which} boundary for outliers.

quest03-quartiles#64.en: Build the boundary. Tap a piece to drop it into the next box.

quest03-quartiles#65.en: Below Q1 for the lower boundary, above Q3 for the upper — always 1,5 × IQR.

quest03-quartiles#66.en: Now calculate the boundary itself (1 decimal).

quest03-quartiles#70.en: Find the IQR first, then go 1,5 × IQR beyond the quartile (below Q1, or above Q3).

quest03-quartiles#76.en: A data set has Q1 = ${q1} and Q3 = ${q3}. Is the value ${x} an outlier?

quest03-quartiles#77.en: Yes — it lies outside the boundaries

quest03-quartiles#78.en: No — it lies within the boundaries

quest03-quartiles#79.en: Find the boundaries Q1 − 1,5×IQR and Q3 + 1,5×IQR. A value beyond them is an outlier.

quest03-quartiles#85.en: A data set has ${n} values in order. Calculate the position of the ${p}th percentile.

quest04-skewness#7.en: The box and whiskers are balanced about the median → symmetric.

quest04-skewness#8.en: The longer half and whisker (the tail) is on the ${skew} → skewed ${skew}.

quest04-skewness#9.en: Look at the box-and-whisker plot. How is the distribution skewed?

quest04-skewness#11.en: The skew is named for the tail — the longer whisker / bigger half.

quest04-skewness#12.en: The bars are roughly symmetric about the centre → normal.

quest04-skewness#13.en: The tall bars are on the ${skew === "right" ? "left" : "right"} and the low tail stretches ${skew} → skewed ${skew}.

quest04-skewness#14.en: Look at the histogram. How is the distribution skewed?

quest04-skewness#16.en: Find the long low tail — the skew is named for it.

quest04-skewness#18.en: The curve rises steeply early then flattens at the top — the thin tail is on the right → skewed right.

quest04-skewness#19.en: The curve stays flat then rises steeply at the top — the thin tail is on the left → skewed left.

quest04-skewness#20.en: Look at the ogive. How is the distribution skewed?

quest04-skewness#22.en: The flat end of the ogive is the tail.

quest04-skewness#26.en: For a data set, the mean x̄ = ${m} and the median = ${med}. How is it skewed?

quest04-skewness#27.en: Compare the mean and median — the mean is pulled toward the tail.

quest04-skewness#28.en: ${rel} → ${skew === "normal" ? "symmetric" : "skewed " + skew} (the mean is pulled toward the tail).

quest04-skewness#29.en: Most of the data is bunched together, with a long thin tail to the ${dir}. How is the distribution described?

quest04-skewness#30.en: The skew is named for the tail.

quest04-skewness#31.en: The tail points ${dir} → skewed to the ${dir}.

quest04-skewness#32.en: Which statement is true for a distribution that is ${skew === "normal" ? "symmetric (normal)" : "skewed to the " + skew}?

quest04-skewness#33.en: Skew toward the tail pulls the mean past the median.

quest05-grouped#1.en: ${freqTable(classes, { total: false })}What is n (the total frequency, Σf)?

quest05-grouped#5.en: What is the midpoint of the class ${lo} ≤ x < ${up}?

quest05-grouped#9.en: For the class ${lo} ≤ x < ${up} with frequency ${f}, calculate f × x (frequency × midpoint).

quest05-grouped#10.en: First find the midpoint x = (lower + upper)/2, then multiply by the frequency.

quest05-grouped#13.en: ${freqTable(classes, { mid: true })}Calculate the estimated mean (to 2 decimal places).

quest05-grouped#14.en: Estimated mean = Σ(f × x) / n. Use each class midpoint x.

quest05-grouped#20.en: The modal class has the highest frequency.

quest05-grouped#21.en: ${correct} has the highest frequency → modal class.

quest05-grouped#22.en: ${freqTable(classes, { cum: true })}The median is at position n/2 = ${C(pos)}. Which is the median class?

quest05-grouped#23.en: Build up the cumulative frequency until you pass position n/2.

quest05-grouped#24.en: Position ${C(pos)} falls in ${correct} (where the cumulative frequency first reaches it).

quest05-grouped#25.en: To get the estimated mean on the calculator with frequency ON, what do you enter into the two columns?

quest05-grouped#26.en: The midpoints in X and the frequencies in FREQ

quest05-grouped#27.en: The frequencies in X and the midpoints in FREQ

quest05-grouped#28.en: The class boundaries in X and the totals in FREQ

quest05-grouped#30.en: Each class is represented by its midpoint, occurring f times.

quest05-grouped#31.en: Midpoints go in the X column, frequencies in the FREQ column, then read x̄ (Var → 2).

quest06-ogives#1.en: For the class ${lo} < x ≤ ${up} with a cumulative frequency of ${cf}, which point do you plot on the ogive?

quest06-ogives#2.en: Plot at (upper boundary of the class ; cumulative frequency).

quest06-ogives#4.en: An ogive’s first class is ${lo} < x ≤ ${up}. At which point is the curve anchored (started at height 0)?

quest06-ogives#5.en: Anchor at the LOWER boundary of the first class, at cumulative frequency 0.

quest06-ogives#6.en: Anchor at (lower boundary of the first class ; 0) = (${lo} ; 0).

quest06-ogives#7.en: ${freqTable(classes, { notation: "lt", total: false })}What is the cumulative frequency up to and including the class ${classInterval(classes[k - 1], "lt")}?

quest06-ogives#8.en: Cumulative frequency is the running total of the frequencies.

quest06-ogives#9.en: Add the frequencies up to that class = ${cum}.

quest06-ogives#11.en: On the ogive, the modal class is the steepest part. Which class interval is it?

quest06-ogives#12.en: The steepest rise = the biggest jump in cumulative frequency = the most data.

quest06-ogives#13.en: The steepest section is ${correct} — the class with the most values.

quest06-ogives#20.en: Use the ogive to read off the ${name}. (n = ${n}.)

quest06-ogives#21.en: Find position ${C(level)} on the cumulative axis, read across to the curve, then straight down.

quest06-ogives#22.en: Position = ${formula} = ${C(level)}; read across to the curve and down → ≈ ${Math.round(val)}.

quest06-ogives#24.en: Use the ogive to read off the ${p}th percentile. (n = ${n}.)

quest06-ogives#25.en: The ${p}th percentile is at position n × ${p}/100 = ${C(level)} on the cumulative axis.

quest06-ogives#26.en: Position = n × ${p}/100 = ${C(level)}; read across and down → ≈ ${Math.round(val)}.

quest06-ogives#28.en: Use the ogive: about how many data values are at most ${X}?

quest06-ogives#29.en: Go up from ${X} on the horizontal axis to the curve, then across to the cumulative-frequency axis.

quest06-ogives#30.en: Read up from ${X} to the curve, then across → ≈ ${Math.round(cumAt)}.

quest07-stddev#2.en: How spread out the data is around the mean

quest07-stddev#3.en: The middle value of the data

quest07-stddev#5.en: The total of all the values

quest07-stddev#6.en: A bigger σ means more spread; a smaller σ means more consistent.

quest07-stddev#7.en: The Var menu reads 1:n 2:x̄ 3:σx 4:sx. Which do you use for the standard deviation?

quest07-stddev#12.en: Use the population standard deviation σx — option 3.

quest07-stddev#15.en: A data set has standard deviation σ = ${sd}. Calculate the variance.

quest07-stddev#16.en: Variance is the standard deviation squared.

quest07-stddev#18.en: A data set has variance ${v}. Calculate the standard deviation.

quest07-stddev#19.en: Standard deviation is the square root of the variance.

quest07-stddev#24.en: A data set has mean x̄ = ${m} and standard deviation σ = ${sd}. Calculate the ${which} boundary (one σ ${which === "lower" ? "below" : "above"} the mean).

quest07-stddev#30.en:
A data set:
${list(data)}
Here x̄ ≈ ${C(mR)} and σ ≈ ${C(sdR)}. How many values lie within one standard deviation of the mean?

quest07-stddev#31.en: Work out x̄ − σ and x̄ + σ, then count the values between them.

quest07-stddev#32.en: lower = x̄ − σ ≈ ${C(Math.round((mR - sdR) * 10) / 10)};  upper = x̄ + σ ≈ ${C(Math.round((mR + sdR) * 10) / 10)}

quest07-stddev#34.en: Count the values inside that interval → ${count}.

quest07-stddev#37.en: Set P has σ = ${C(a)} and Set Q has σ = ${C(b)}. Which set is more consistent?

quest07-stddev#39.en: More consistent = less spread = the SMALLER standard deviation.

quest07-stddev#40.en: ${better} has the smaller σ, so its data is more consistent.

quest08-mixed#11.en: Every value in a data set is increased by ${k}. What happens to the ${m.name}?

quest08-mixed#12.en: Adding the same number to every value shifts the centre but not the spread.

quest08-mixed#14.en: Spread is unchanged — the ${m.name} stays the same.

quest08-mixed#15.en: The mean of a data set is ${M}. If ${k} is ${add ? "added to" : "subtracted from"} every value, what is the new mean?

quest08-mixed#16.en: The mean shifts by the same amount you add to (or subtract from) every value.

quest08-mixed#19.en: A data set has standard deviation σ = ${C(sd)}. Every value is increased by ${k}. What is the new standard deviation?

quest08-mixed#20.en: Shifting every value sideways does not change how spread out the data is.

quest08-mixed#21.en: Adding a constant leaves the spread unchanged → σ stays ${C(sd)}.

quest08-mixed#26.en: The median is the line inside each box — which sits further right?

quest08-mixed#27.en: ${correct} has its median line further along the scale.

quest08-mixed#28.en: Which set is more spread out (larger range)?

quest08-mixed#30.en: Range = distance from the left whisker end to the right whisker end.

quest08-mixed#31.en: ${correct} stretches further from minimum to maximum → larger range.

quest08-mixed#32.en: A data set has an IQR of ${iqrV} and Q1 = ${q1}. Find Q3.

quest08-mixed#33.en: IQR = Q3 − Q1, so Q3 = Q1 + IQR.

quest08-mixed#36.en: A data set has an IQR of ${iqrV} and Q3 = ${q3}. Find Q1.

quest08-mixed#37.en: IQR = Q3 − Q1, so Q1 = Q3 − IQR.

quest08-mixed#39.en: A data set has variance ${v}. Every value is increased by ${k}. What is the new variance?

quest08-mixed#40.en: Adding a constant doesn’t change the spread — so the variance is unchanged.

quest08-mixed#41.en: Adding a constant leaves the spread unchanged → variance stays ${v}.
